levels.title: The White-Haired Child
levels.teaser: Before the hero comes his father: a baby abandoned on a mountain and raised by a wondrous bird.
story: A thousand years ago the Persian poet Ferdowsi gathered the old legends of Iran into one vast poem, the Shahnameh, or Book of Kings. Its greatest hero is Rostam, but his story begins before his birth, with his grandfather Sam. Sam was the most trusted champion of King Manuchehr of Iran, and he ruled the province of Zabolestan, also called Sistan, in the south-east of the kingdom. He had everything a man could want except a child.

At last a son was born to him, strong and beautiful, but with hair as white as an old man's. For days nobody dared to tell Sam. When he finally saw the baby he was filled with shame. He feared that the nobles would laugh at him and whisper that the boy was the child of a demon. So he gave a cruel order: the baby was to be carried far away and left alone on the slopes of Mount Alborz, a peak so high that it seemed to touch the stars.

On that mountain lived the Simurgh, a huge and wise bird. Flying out to find food for her chicks, she saw the infant crying on the bare rock, and she carried him up to her nest. But pity entered her heart, and instead of feeding him to her young she raised him among them. Years passed. The boy grew into a tall young man, and travellers began to carry tales of him down into the world.

Sam, meanwhile, was troubled by dreams that reproached him for throwing away the gift God had given him. Full of remorse, he journeyed to Mount Alborz and prayed for forgiveness. The Simurgh saw him and understood why he had come. She told the young man that it was time to return to his own kind, and she gave him feathers from her own wing. If ever he was in desperate trouble, he had only to burn one and she would come. Sam embraced his son, begged his pardon, and named him Zal. The king welcomed the young man kindly, and Sam left him to govern Zabolestan.

On his travels Zal came to Kabul, a small kingdom that paid tribute to Sam. Its king, Mehrab, was handsome and courteous, but he was descended from Zahhak, the serpent-shouldered tyrant who had once oppressed Iran. Zal heard a description of Mehrab's daughter, Rudabeh, and fell in love with her before he had ever seen her. Rudabeh, hearing her father praise Zal, lost her heart in the same way. Her maids carried messages between them and arranged a secret meeting.

By night Zal came to the foot of her palace wall. From the roof Rudabeh loosened her long black hair and let it down for him to climb. Zal would not do it; he kissed the dark tresses and said he would never harm them. Instead he threw up his lasso, caught the battlements, and climbed the rope. There the two pledged themselves to each other.

Their secret did not last, and almost everyone opposed the match. Mehrab was furious and afraid. King Manuchehr dreaded what a child with the blood of Zahhak and the strength of Sam might become, and he ordered Sam to march against Kabul. Zal pleaded with his father, reminding him of the wrong he had once done his son, and Sam sent him to the king with a letter. Rudabeh's mother, Sindokht, went bravely to Sam as an envoy to plead for her city. Then the king's astrologers studied the stars and announced that from this marriage would come a champion who would be the shield of Iran. The king's wise men tested Zal with riddles, he answered every one, and Manuchehr gave his consent. Zal and Rudabeh were married in Kabul.

In time Rudabeh was with child, but the child was so large that she suffered terribly. One day she fainted from the pain, and the household feared she would die. Zal remembered the Simurgh's promise and burned a feather. At once the great bird appeared. She told him to dry his tears, and gave careful instructions. A skilled priest must bring a sharp blade. Rudabeh should first be made drowsy with wine. Then her side should be cut open, the child lifted out, and the wound sewn up. Finally a herb crushed with milk and musk should be laid on the wound, and it should be stroked with the Simurgh's feather.

All was done as she said. The boy was as big as a lion cub, and everyone who saw him marvelled. When Rudabeh woke and saw her son she smiled and said that she was delivered from her pain. In Persian the word she used was rastam, and so the child was named Rostam. Ten nurses were needed to feed him. A likeness of the baby was sewn from silk and sent to his grandfather Sam, who gave thanks. The champion the stars had promised had arrived.

levels.title: The Boy, the Mace and the Horse
levels.teaser: A young giant needs a horse strong enough to carry him, and Iran needs a king.
story: Rostam grew at a pace that astonished everyone in Zabolestan. Ferdowsi tells us that once he was weaned he ate as much as five grown men. While still a boy he had the height and the shoulders of a warrior, and his grandfather Sam travelled a long way simply to look at him and wonder.

One night, while the household slept, there was shouting in the streets. The white elephant belonging to his father Zal had broken its chains and was rampaging through the town. Rostam woke, snatched up the heavy mace that had belonged to Sam, and ran for the door. The guards barred his way, afraid of what Zal would say if they let his young son out into such danger. Rostam knocked the gatekeeper aside, broke the fastening of the gate, and went out alone. The elephant charged at him like a moving hill. Rostam roared back at it, struck it a single blow on the head with the mace, and the beast fell dead. Then he went back to bed. In the morning Zal heard the story and knew what kind of son he had.

Iran at that time was in grave trouble. Across the river Oxus lay Turan, the rival kingdom of the northern steppes, and its fiercest prince was Afrasiab. Afrasiab had invaded Iran, and had captured and killed the Iranian king Nowzar. The short reigns that followed left the throne empty and the country open to attack. The nobles came to Zal for help. Zal told them that he was growing old, but that his son, though young, had the heart of a lion.

Rostam said that he was made for battle, not for feasting, and asked for two things: a mace and a horse. The mace was easy, for Zal gave him the great mace of Sam. The horse was harder. Whenever Rostam tested a horse he pressed his hand down on its back, and each one buckled until its belly touched the ground. So Zal ordered the herds of Zabolestan and Kabul to be driven past his son, one after another.

Among the herds from Kabul came a grey mare, and behind her a colt with the chest of a lion. His coat was dappled red and gold, like rose petals scattered over saffron. Rostam readied his lasso, but the old herdsman called out a warning. Nobody knew who owned this colt, he said. He had been fit for the saddle for three years, and people simply called him Rostam's Rakhsh. But whenever anyone came near him, his mother attacked like a lioness.

Rostam threw his lasso over the colt's head. The mare charged with her teeth bared. Rostam gave a shout that stopped her short and struck her with his fist, and she turned and fled back to the herd. Then he pressed his hand on the colt's back with all his strength. The back did not bend. Rostam asked the price. If you are Rostam, the herdsman answered, then the price of this horse is the land of Iran; mount him and set the country right. From that day Rakhsh carried Rostam through every adventure of his long life.

His first task came at once. The priests told Zal that a descendant of the ancient king Feridun, a man named Kay Qobad, was living near Mount Alborz and was worthy of the crown. Zal sent Rostam to bring him. Rostam fought his way through the Turanian outposts and came to a pleasant place of trees and running water, where a company of young men were feasting beside a stream. They invited him to sit and drink. He replied that he had no time, for he was seeking Kay Qobad. The host smiled and revealed that he himself was Kay Qobad. The night before, he said, he had dreamed that two white falcons flew to him from Iran, carrying a crown as bright as the sun. The two rode for Iran without delay, and when a Turanian warrior named Qalun blocked their road with his men, Rostam scattered them. Kay Qobad was crowned king.

Then came the battle with Turan. Rostam asked his father to point out Afrasiab, and Zal showed him the black banner. Rostam charged straight for it, seized Afrasiab by the belt, and lifted him clean out of the saddle, meaning to carry him as a prisoner to Kay Qobad. But the belt could not take the weight. It snapped, Afrasiab fell to the ground, and his horsemen closed around him and carried him to safety.

The Turanian army broke all the same. Afrasiab, shaken by what he had met, urged his father to make peace, and the Oxus became the border between the two kingdoms once more. Iran had a king again, and a new champion. But Afrasiab had escaped, and he would trouble Rostam and Iran for many years to come.

levels.title: The Seven Labours
levels.teaser: A foolish king is a prisoner in a land of demons, and only one rider takes the short, deadly road to reach him.
story: After Kay Qobad, his son Kay Kavus became king of Iran. He was brave, but vain and reckless. One day a div, a demon, came to court disguised as a minstrel and sang of Mazandaran, a land where it was always spring. In the Shahnameh, Mazandaran is a country of demons and sorcerers. Kavus decided to conquer it. Zal rode to court to talk him out of it, in vain.

At first Kavus plundered as he pleased. Then the king of Mazandaran called on the mightiest of the demons, the White Div. In the night a black cloud settled over the Iranian camp, and by morning Kavus and most of his men were blind. They were held captive under the guard of a demon chief named Arzhang. Kavus managed to send a message to Zal. Zal told Rostam there were two roads to Mazandaran: the long, safe one the king had taken, and a short one full of lions, demons and darkness. Rostam chose the short road.

First labour. Rostam lay down to sleep in a reed bed that was in fact a lion's lair. The lion came home and sprang at Rakhsh, but the horse struck it with his hooves, sank his teeth into its back, and killed it. Rostam woke and scolded him: if Rakhsh had died, how would he carry his heavy arms to Mazandaran on foot?

Second labour. The road crossed a burning desert with no water. Rostam staggered, his tongue cracked with thirst, and he prayed. Then a well-fed ram crossed his path. Reasoning that such an animal must drink somewhere, Rostam followed it to a spring. He gave thanks and blessed the ram. Before sleeping he told Rakhsh not to fight anything alone again, but to wake him.

Third labour. The spring was the haunt of a dragon. In the night it crept close, and Rakhsh stamped to wake his master, but the dragon vanished into the dark and Rostam saw nothing. It happened a second time, and Rostam angrily threatened to cut off the horse's head if he was woken again for nothing. The third time Rakhsh, torn between fear of the dragon and fear of his master, woke him once more, and now the dragon could not hide. Rostam fought it, and when Rakhsh saw his master hard pressed he tore at the dragon's shoulder with his teeth. Rostam struck off its head.

Fourth labour. Beside a stream Rostam found a meal laid out: roast meat, bread, wine and a lute. It was a feast of sorcerers, who had fled at his approach. He sat down, took up the lute, and sang about his hard, wandering life. A witch heard him, took the form of a beautiful young woman, and sat at his side. Rostam, pouring wine, gave praise to God. At the name of God her face turned black. He caught her in his lasso and demanded her true shape, and she became a withered hag. He cut her in two.

Fifth labour. Rostam passed through a land of total darkness, giving Rakhsh the reins. Coming out into green fields, he lay down to sleep and let Rakhsh graze in the crop. The keeper of the field beat Rostam's feet with a stick, and Rostam, without a word, tore off the man's ears. The keeper ran to his lord, a young chieftain named Olad, who rode out with his men. Rostam scattered them and caught Olad in his lasso. He offered a bargain: guide me truthfully to Kavus and to the White Div, and I will make you king of Mazandaran; lie, and you die. Olad agreed.

Sixth labour. Olad led him to the camp of Arzhang. Rostam gave his battle cry, and when Arzhang rushed from his tent Rostam seized him and tore his head from his body. The other demons fled. In the city Rakhsh neighed like thunder, and the blind Kavus knew that Rostam had come. The king told him that only the blood of the White Div could cure their blindness.

Seventh labour. Olad advised him that demons sleep when the sun is hot, so Rostam waited for full day. He tied Olad to a tree and entered a cave as black as a pit. When his eyes cleared he made out a shape like a mountain, white-haired and asleep. Rostam would not strike a sleeper; he shouted to wake him. The White Div came at him with a millstone. Rostam cut off one of its legs, and even so they wrestled until the ground was mud with blood. At last Rostam lifted the demon, dashed him down, and drove in his dagger.

The blood was dripped into the eyes of Kavus and his men, and they saw again. The king of Mazandaran was defeated, and Rostam kept his word: Olad was made ruler of the land. These seven trials are known in Persian as the Haft Khan.

levels.title: Rostam and Sohrab
levels.teaser: A lost horse leads Rostam to a border town, and to the deepest sorrow of his life.
story: One day Rostam went hunting alone near the border of Turan. He roasted a wild ass, ate, and fell asleep, leaving Rakhsh to graze. A band of Turanian horsemen came upon the famous horse, and after a hard struggle they caught him with their lassos and led him away. Rostam woke to find him gone. Carrying his saddle and weapons, he followed the tracks on foot to Samangan, a small kingdom on the frontier. Its king welcomed him with honour, promised that Rakhsh would be found, and gave a feast.

That night the door of Rostam's chamber opened quietly. A servant entered with a lamp, and behind came a young woman: Tahmineh, the king's daughter. She told him that she had heard the tales of his deeds and had long wished to be his wife and to bear his child. Rostam sent a priest to ask her father for her hand that same night, and the king gladly agreed.

At dawn Rostam took from his arm a jewel known to all the world as his and gave it to Tahmineh. If their child was a girl, she was to braid it in her hair. If it was a boy, she was to bind it on his arm as his father's token. Rakhsh was brought back, and Rostam rode home to Zabolestan. He told no one what had happened.

Tahmineh bore a son and named him Sohrab. By the age of ten no one in the land could wrestle him. He demanded to know who his father was, and his mother told him, warning him to keep it secret from Afrasiab, Rostam's old enemy. Sohrab formed a grand plan. He would lead an army into Iran, overthrow Kay Kavus and set Rostam on the throne, and then return to take Afrasiab's crown as well.

Afrasiab heard and was delighted. He sent troops and two commanders, Human and Barman, with secret orders that father and son must never recognise each other. Perhaps the young lion would kill the old one, and then Sohrab himself could be dealt with. Sohrab crossed the border and attacked the White Fortress. He captured its champion, Hojir. Then Gordafarid, a daughter of the fortress, hid her hair under a helmet and rode out to fight him. In the struggle her helmet came off and her hair spilled free. Sohrab was amazed. She tricked him with a promise of surrender, slipped back through the gate, and mocked him from the wall.

Kay Kavus summoned Rostam urgently. Rostam, untroubled, spent some days feasting before he came. The king flew into a rage and ordered him hanged. Rostam strode out, declaring that he was no man's slave, and only the pleading of the old noble Gudarz made peace. The army marched. Sohrab, from a hilltop, asked his captive Hojir to name the owner of each Iranian tent. Hojir, afraid for Rostam, lied and said he did not see Rostam's tent among them.

Rostam and Sohrab met alone between the two armies. They fought with spears, swords and maces until their weapons were broken and their horses exhausted. Sohrab felt strangely drawn to the old warrior and asked him directly whether he was Rostam. Rostam denied it, saying he was only a lesser man.

The next day they wrestled. Sohrab threw Rostam to the ground, sat on his chest, and drew his dagger. Rostam saved himself by cunning. Among us, he said, the custom is that a champion does not kill at the first fall, only at the second. Sohrab let him go. Human told the young man he had been a fool. Rostam washed in a stream and prayed for strength.

When they wrestled again, Rostam seized Sohrab, bent his back, and threw him. Knowing the young man would not stay down, he drew his blade at once and stabbed him in the chest. Sohrab said that he had come seeking his father, and that when Rostam learned of his death he would avenge it, even if the killer became a fish in the sea. The world went dark before Rostam's eyes. He asked for proof. Sohrab told him to open his armour, and there on his arm was the jewel Rostam had given Tahmineh.

Rostam tore his clothes and would have killed himself had the nobles not held him back. Sohrab asked only that the Turanian army be allowed to go home unharmed. Rostam sent Gudarz to Kay Kavus to beg for the nushdaru, a healing potion kept in the royal treasury. Kavus, fearing what such a father and son might do together, refused. Rostam set out to plead in person, but a messenger overtook him: Sohrab was dead. Rostam burned his own tent and carried his son's coffin home to Zabolestan.

levels.title: The Blood of Siavash
levels.teaser: Rostam raises a prince who keeps his word when kings do not, and pays for it in a foreign land.
story: Kay Kavus had a son named Siavash, a child so fine that the whole court spoke of him. Rostam came to the king and asked to bring the boy up himself. He took Siavash to Zabolestan and taught him everything a prince should know: riding, archery, the lasso, how to lead an army, how to behave at a feast, and how to judge justly. Siavash returned to his father as a young man, admired by all.

The king's wife, Sudabeh, fell in love with her stepson. She summoned him to the women's quarters and declared her desire. Siavash, loyal to his father, refused her. Afraid of being exposed, Sudabeh tore her clothes and cried out that he had attacked her. Kavus was torn between his wife and his son, and the priests advised a trial by fire.

A mountain of firewood was heaped up in two great piles with a narrow path between them, and set alight. Siavash, dressed in white and riding his black horse, galloped into the flames. The crowd wept. Then he rode out at the far end unharmed and smiling. Kavus wanted to have Sudabeh executed, but Siavash, knowing his father would later regret it, begged for her life, and she was pardoned.

Soon afterwards Afrasiab of Turan invaded again. Siavash, glad to leave the court, asked for command of the army, and Rostam went with him. They took the city of Balkh. Then Afrasiab had a terrible dream of his own ruin. Frightened, he asked for peace, sent rich gifts, and handed over a hundred of his own kinsmen as hostages. Siavash and Rostam accepted, and Siavash gave his oath.

Rostam carried the news to Kavus. The king was furious. He ordered that the hostages be sent to him for execution and that the war go on, and he accused Rostam of having grown soft. Rostam, insulted, rode home to Sistan. Siavash now faced an impossible choice. He would not break his oath or send the hostages to their deaths, and he could not go home in disobedience. He returned the hostages to Afrasiab, handed over the army, and crossed the river into Turan.

There Piran, Afrasiab's wise old commander, welcomed him like a son, and Afrasiab too came to love him. Siavash married Piran's daughter Jarireh, and later Farangis, the daughter of Afrasiab himself. He was given a province and built a beautiful city, Siavashgerd. But Afrasiab's brother Garsivaz was envious. He told the king that Siavash was plotting with Iran, and he told Siavash that the king meant him harm, until each man feared the other.

Afrasiab marched against him. Siavash, still bound by his oath, would not fight. His few Iranian companions were killed, and he was seized, dragged away, and put to death at Garsivaz's urging. It is said that where his blood fell a plant sprang up, which people called the blood of Siavash. Piran had been away and arrived too late to save him. He was just in time to save Farangis, who was carrying Siavash's child. She gave birth to a son, Kay Khosrow, and he was hidden among shepherds.

When the news reached Iran, the whole country mourned. Rostam's grief turned to fury. He rode to court and told Kavus to his face that his bad temper and his love for Sudabeh had destroyed his son. Then he strode into the women's quarters, dragged Sudabeh out, and killed her. Kavus did not stir from his throne.

Rostam led the armies of Iran into Turan, with his own son Faramarz commanding the vanguard. A son of Afrasiab named Sorkheh was captured, and on Rostam's order he was killed as Siavash had been killed. Afrasiab was beaten in battle and fled, and for some years Rostam himself sat on the throne of Turan. But vengeance could not bring Siavash back, and in the end the Iranians went home and Afrasiab returned.

Hope came from another direction. The old noble Gudarz dreamed that a prince of Iran was alive in Turan. His son Giv searched alone for seven years, found Kay Khosrow, and brought him and his mother Farangis across the Oxus to Iran. Kay Khosrow became the most just of kings. Rostam served him as champion, and among his deeds in that reign was the rescue of Giv's son Bizhan from the pit where Afrasiab had thrown him for loving Manizheh, Afrasiab's daughter. It was Kay Khosrow who finally brought the long war for Siavash to its end.

levels.title: Rostam and Esfandiyar
levels.teaser: A king who will not give up his crown sends his own son to put the old hero in chains.
story: Years passed, for in the Shahnameh Rostam lives for centuries. Kay Khosrow gave up his throne to Lohrasp, and now Lohrasp's son Goshtasp sat on the throne of Iran. He had adopted the faith taught by the prophet Zoroaster, and his son Esfandiyar was its champion. Esfandiyar was the finest warrior of his generation, and it was said that no weapon could wound his body. He had won his father's wars against Turan and had rescued his own sisters from an enemy fortress. Again and again Goshtasp promised him the throne as a reward, and again and again he broke his word.

At last Esfandiyar demanded the crown outright. Goshtasp consulted his counsellor Jamasp, who could read the future, and learned that Esfandiyar was fated to die in Zabolestan at the hand of Rostam. Then the king set his son a final condition. Rostam, he said, had grown proud and no longer came to court to pay homage. Go to Zabolestan and bring him here in chains, and the crown is yours. Esfandiyar saw that the order was unjust and said so, for Rostam had served the kings of Iran all his life. But he was a prince who obeyed. His mother, Katayun, wept and begged him not to go.

On the road the lead camel of his caravan lay down and would not get up. It was an ill omen. Esfandiyar had the animal killed and marched on, but his heart was uneasy. He camped by the river Hirmand and sent his son Bahman ahead with his message. Bahman found Rostam out hunting, and from a hilltop he rolled a boulder down at him. Rostam waited until it was almost upon him, then kicked it aside with his heel. He received the young man kindly all the same.

Rostam's answer was generous. He would welcome the prince as a guest, give him treasure, and ride beside him to court to accept the king's judgement. One thing only he would never do. No one had ever seen Rostam in chains, and no one ever would. Esfandiyar was just as firmly bound by his father's command. The two men met, and each admired the other, but neither would yield.

So they fought. Rostam's arrows glanced off Esfandiyar, while Esfandiyar's arrows pierced Rostam and Rakhsh again and again. Meanwhile fighting broke out between their followers, and two of Esfandiyar's sons were killed by Rostam's brother Zavareh and his son Faramarz. By evening Rostam, badly wounded, let Rakhsh go home alone and climbed a rocky height on foot. He asked for a truce until morning. Then he crossed the river and reached his house, bleeding.

Zal despaired when he saw his son and the horse. Then he remembered the Simurgh. He climbed to a high place and burned her feather, and the great bird came out of the darkness. She drew the arrowheads from Rostam and from Rakhsh and stroked their wounds with her feathers, and they were healed. But she gave Rostam a warning. Whoever sheds the blood of Esfandiyar, she said, will be hunted down by fate; he will have no peace in this world and suffering in the next. It would be best to make peace. Rostam answered that he would accept death before the shame of chains.

So that same night the Simurgh guided him to a distant shore where a tamarisk tree grew. She told him to choose a straight branch, straighten it in the fire, fit it with an arrowhead and feathers, and steep it in wine. He must aim for Esfandiyar's eyes, for only there could the prince be hurt.

In the morning Esfandiyar was astonished to see Rostam and Rakhsh whole again, and suspected the sorcery of Zal. Rostam pleaded with him one last time. He offered everything he owned and every honour except the chains, and he called on God to witness that he did not want this fight. Esfandiyar gave the same answer as before: chains or battle. Then Rostam set the tamarisk arrow to his bow and loosed it. It struck Esfandiyar in the eyes. The prince slumped forward over the mane of his black horse and fell to the ground.

Esfandiyar did not die at once. To his brother Pashutan and his son Bahman he said that it was not Rostam who had killed him, nor the Simurgh, nor the arrow. It was his father Goshtasp, who had sent him to his death in order to keep the crown. Then he asked Rostam to take Bahman into his house and bring him up as a prince should be raised, and Rostam gave his promise.
Pashutan carried his brother's coffin back to court and reproached the king before all the nobles. Rostam returned to Zabolestan with the Simurgh's warning in his ears.

levels.title: The Death of Rostam
levels.teaser: No enemy ever defeated Rostam in the field; the last danger comes from inside his own family.
story: Late in his life Zal had another son, born to a servant woman of his household. The boy was named Shaghad. When the astrologers read his stars they were dismayed: this child, they said, would bring ruin on the house of Sam. Zal grieved and prayed that it might not be so. When Shaghad was grown, Zal sent him to the king of Kabul. There he became a fine horseman, and the king gave him his daughter in marriage.

Every year Kabul paid a tribute to Rostam. The king of Kabul had hoped that, with Rostam's half-brother as his son-in-law, the tribute would be forgotten. But when the time came, Rostam's men arrived and collected it as they always had. Shaghad took this as a humiliation. He went to the king in private and said that his brother showed him no respect, and that together they should set a trap for him.

This was their plan. At a feast the king would insult Shaghad in front of everyone. Shaghad would ride to Zabolestan and complain, and Rostam would come to punish the king. Meanwhile the king would have pits dug in his hunting ground, each deep enough to swallow a horse and rider. Their floors would be planted with spears and swords, points upward, and their mouths covered over so that nothing showed.

It was done. Shaghad came to Rostam and told how the king of Kabul had mocked him and his family. Rostam was angry. He promised to cast the king down and put Shaghad on the throne of Kabul, and he began to gather an army. Shaghad told him there was no need: the king already regretted his words, and a small escort would be enough. So Rostam set out with his brother Zavareh and only a few men.

The king of Kabul came to meet them barefoot and bareheaded, begging forgiveness and blaming the wine. Rostam forgave him. A feast was spread in a green meadow, and afterwards the king spoke of a hunting ground nearby, full of deer and wild asses. Rostam had loved the hunt all his life, and he agreed to go.

The hunters scattered. Rostam, Zavareh and Shaghad rode toward the place where the pits lay hidden. Rakhsh smelled the freshly turned earth. He reared, picked his way forward carefully, and then refused to go further. Rostam's judgement was clouded that day. Impatient with his horse, he touched him lightly with the whip. Rakhsh sprang forward and fell into a pit. The blades tore the horse's body and pierced Rostam's chest and legs.

With the last of his great strength Rostam dragged himself up to the rim of the pit. He saw Shaghad standing there and understood. Shaghad told him that he had shed blood enough in his long life and that his time had come. The king of Kabul arrived, pretended to weep, and offered to send for physicians. Rostam answered that the time for physicians was past, that no one lives for ever, and that his son Faramarz would call the king to account for his blood.

Then Rostam asked his half-brother for one favour. String my bow, he said, and lay it beside me with two arrows, so that if a lion comes while I am still breathing I may defend myself. Shaghad, smiling, strung the bow and set it down. But when he saw Rostam lift it he was afraid, and he hid behind an old plane tree whose trunk was hollow. Rostam drew the bow, wounded as he was, and loosed. The arrow passed through the tree and through the man behind it, and pinned the two together. Shaghad cried out and died. Rostam gave thanks to God that he had been granted the strength to avenge himself before his own death. Then he died. Zavareh had fallen into another pit, and he died too.

One of the escort escaped and carried the news to Zal. Faramarz came with an army, raised the bodies from the pits, and laid them in coffins. Mourners passed Rostam's coffin from hand to hand all the way home to Zabolestan. Rakhsh was brought home as well and buried beside his master's tomb. Then Faramarz marched on Kabul and put its king to death. Rudabeh, Rostam's mother, grieved so deeply that for a time she lost her reason.

So ended the life of Rostam, the son of Zal, who had guarded the throne of Iran through the reigns of many kings. He is still, a thousand years after Ferdowsi wrote, the best-loved hero of the Persian-speaking world.

finale.title: Where is Prince Mohsey?
story: When Rostam died, the Simurgh flew one last time over Zabolestan. Zal, now very old, stood at his window and watched her circle the house where his son had grown up. She did not land. She let a single feather fall onto his windowsill, and he heard her voice as clearly as on the day she had carried him down from Mount Alborz.
“This is my last feather for your family,” she said. “Do not burn it for war. Keep it for a child of Iran who is lost, as you were once lost. When it is burned, I will come one final time.”

Zal laid the feather in a box of sandalwood. The box passed from hand to hand for centuries, from the house of Sam to the kings of Iran, the heirs of Iraj, and it was kept in the royal treasury long after anyone remembered what it was for. Rostam’s battles became songs, the songs became a book, and the book became the Shahnameh.

In time a prince was born in that royal house and named Mohsey. As a boy he read the Book of Kings until the candles burned out. He knew every labour of Rostam and every line of Fereydun’s division of the world. And he could never sit still. He climbed the palace walls to look at the horizon, and he asked every traveller what lay beyond it.

When he came of age he told his family that he wanted to see the world. His grandmother, the queen mother, did not argue. She opened the treasury, took out the sandalwood box and put it in his hands. “This is not for when you are tired or sad,” she said. “It is only for when you are truly lost.”

Mohsey rode west. He crossed rivers and deserts, slept in caravanserais and under the stars, and learned a little of every language on the road. Then, high in the mountains, a storm came down on him. Snow hid the path and the night hid the snow. His horse stopped and would not go on. For the first time in his life Mohsey did not know which way was home and which way was forward.
He opened the box, struck a spark and burned the last feather. Out of the storm came a sound like a great wind, and the Simurgh settled on the rocks beside him, her feathers glowing like coals.

“I raised a lost child once,” she said. “His name was Zal. I will not carry you home, Prince of Iran. Home is behind you. What you are looking for is ahead. Ride down into Rum, find the great river that runs east to the Black Sea, and follow it against the current until you reach a city where white horses dance. You will know the rest when you see it.” Before he could thank her, she was gone, and the storm with her.

So Mohsey came into Rum, the land Fereydun gave to Salm, whose brother Tur had helped him murder Iraj, the first king of Iran. The guards at the frontier saw the seal of Iraj’s line on his ring and did not know what to do. A thousand years ago their kings had been enemies. But the law of Rum was clear: a prince of a royal house must be brought before the King.

The King of Rum was old and white-bearded, and his eyes were kind. His courtiers whispered as Mohsey bowed before the throne, for they too knew the story of Salm and Iraj. The King raised his hand for silence. “Your ancestor was killed by mine,” he said. “That was a very long time ago. A wise king does not inherit his grandfathers’ quarrels, only their duties. You are welcome here.”

He saw that the young prince was hungry for learning, so he gave him a place at the royal academy in his capital, the city on the great river. There Mohsey studied the languages of the West, the law of kings, the stars, and the long history of Rum.

One afternoon in the great library he took down a copy of the Book of Kings and opened it at the story of Fereydun’s sons. A young woman at the same table was reading the same page in another copy. She looked up and told him, quite firmly, that Salm was not entirely to blame. Mohsey told her, just as firmly, that he certainly was. They argued until the librarian asked them to leave, and they kept arguing all the way down the stairs.

Her name was Softolli. She was a princess of Rum, of the line of Salm, from the green island at the far western edge of Rum, and like him she had come to the capital to study. She was clever, she laughed easily, and she never gave up an argument. Neither did he. They argued again the next day, and the day after that, until neither of them could remember the last day they had not talked.
Where did the prince of Iran find the princess of Rum? The Simurgh left you a fragment of her riddle at the end of every chapter of Rostam’s life. Put the seven fragments together and name the city.

near.austria: The right land, but the Simurgh asked for a city. Which city?
near.osterreich: The right land, but the Simurgh asked for a city. Which city?
near.danube: That is the river. Which city stands on it?
near.donau: That is the river. Which city stands on it?

hints: The Simurgh shakes her head. Read the fragments again: a great river, dancing white horses, a city besieged twice, a dance in three beats.
The river is the Danube, and the white horses are the Lipizzaners of the Spanish Riding School.
Today the city is the capital of Austria.
ending: Vienna. The city on the Danube, where the white horses of the Spanish Riding School dance, where the waltz turns in golden ballrooms, and where the summer palace of Schönbrunn is painted the yellow of saffron.
Twice the armies of the East came to its walls, and twice they turned back. The third time a man came from the East, he came alone, with no army at all, and the city let him in.

Mohsey and Softolli walked by the Danube in every season. They ate Sachertorte in coffee houses with marble tables, still arguing about Salm and Iraj, and they waltzed at a winter ball while the bell in the Steffl rang out over the old town.

When the old King of Rum heard that the prince of Iran and the princess of Rum had chosen each other, he laughed until his crown slipped. “Fereydun divided the world among his sons,” he said, “and their children fought over it for a thousand years. It took two people who would not stop talking to put it back together.”
Far away, on the summit of Mount Alborz, the Simurgh folded her wings. The last feather had done its work. A child of Iran had been lost, and had been found.

So where is Prince Mohsey? He is in Vienna. And he has heard that you have come all this way, through seven chapters and every one of Rostam’s battles, to find him. He is waiting at his table, and he would like a game.
